why: THE IDENTITY-MODIFIER TEST: the modifier wins over the standard preparation — a wrong ingredient sends a hard-constraint diner to food they cannot eat.
THE IDENTITY-MODIFIER TEST: 'white pizza' has no tomato sauce.
THE EXCLUSIVITY TEST: 'marg' is claimed by both the cocktail and the pizza — an alias that fails exclusivity fuses two dishes in search.
Keep-side of the exclusivity line: 'army stew' is an established co-name pointing at nothing but budae jjigae.
Invention-worse-than-silence economics: an ambiguous name has no canonical contents — empty, never a plausible fabrication.
Same economics, second instance: 'seasonal salad' is whatever the kitchen has — an invented list is indistinguishable from a real one forever.
Never invent or shorten a name yourself: 'chicken tikka masala' has no established shorthand to emit — 'ctm' style abbreviations must not be minted.
S4 TRADITION TEST keep-side: 'birria' belongs to Mexican cooking unmistakably, everywhere it is served.
S4 reject-side: 'fried chicken' is shared across traditions — names NO tradition; empty is the cheap error.
S4: identity modifiers govern — 'korean fried chicken' commits to korean even though the bare name is shared.

S4 granularity: the prompt's own example — 'mapo tofu' names the Sichuan repertoire; 'sichuan' must be emitted (a broader 'chinese' beside it is permitted only as a defensible second level, so it is not pinned either way).
S4: the prompt's own keep-side example — 'budae jjigae' -> korean; the tradition travels with the name.
S4: a diet word is never a tradition — 'vegan al pastor taco' is Mexican food; 'vegan' must not appear in cuisines.
S4: an ambiguous menu label entails no tradition — same silence economics as ingredients.
Keep-side control: the standard preparation and the one established alias both come through.
